draft.title: Quality management
card: checking finished products, or outputs, and removing those that fall short of the standard. It finds faults after the work is done.
setting standards for each stage of the process, so faults are less likely to happen. It focuses on how the work is done, not only the end result.
an approach where every worker, in every area of the business, is responsible for quality. It is a whole-of-business culture, not one team's job.
A business may use all three together. Quality control checks the product, quality assurance guides the process, and total quality management spreads the responsibility.
draft.remember: Control checks the output, assurance sets process standards, and total quality management involves everyone.

a.q: A furniture maker wants fewer faults in its chairs. Which action is an example of quality assurance?
opts: Writing standards that every step of production must meet
Inspecting finished chairs and discarding the faulty ones
Returning a faulty batch to the supplier after delivery
Asking only the manager to review customer complaints
a.why: Quality assurance sets standards for the process so faults are less likely. Inspecting finished chairs is quality control, because it checks outputs after they are made.
a.clue: Look for the option about the process, not the finished product.

b.q: At Ravi's bakery in Bendigo, every worker, from the baker to the cashier, must fix quality problems they notice and suggest ways to prevent them. Which approach is this?
b.why: Quality is treated as everyone's job across the whole business, which is total quality management. Quality assurance sets process standards, but it does not on its own make every worker responsible for quality.
b.clue: Who is responsible for quality in this bakery?

a.best: Writing standards that every step of production must meet
